# Publishing and Proving the Rebuild {#sec-publish}



The guide is finished, and nobody but you can see it: every output sits in a folder on your
computer. This chapter puts it on the web, where anyone can open it on a phone, with Git to
keep every version of the source and GitHub Pages to serve the result. Then it asks the
question the whole workflow is built to answer: if one input changes, which outputs change
with it, and how do you know? That question comes with no prompt. It tests whether you can
predict what a rebuild will do, and then check.

## Git: every change, safely {#sec-git}

Chapter 1 likened Git to Word's Track Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history. In
practice that means two things. You see exactly what changed, line by line, and someone else
can approve it before it counts. And every earlier version of the whole project is kept, with
a note saying why it changed, so any of them can be restored or compared.

The vocabulary is short (@fig-git-cycle; Pro Git and GitHub's documentation, checked
2026-10-31). A *repository* is a project folder with its history; each saved version is a
*commit*, a snapshot of every tracked file with its message.

![Every change, safely. A team takes each change round the whole loop; working alone, as in this book, you commit to the main line and push.](../media/diagrams/git-cycle){#fig-git-cycle .on-light fig-alt="Six steps. Branch: work on a branch, so main stays untouched. Commit: save a snapshot of the files with a message saying why. Push: copy the commits to GitHub. Pull request: propose the change and show the difference. Review: someone reads the difference and comments, approves or asks for changes. Merge: the commits join main. Working alone, you commit to main and push; in a team, every change goes round the whole loop."}

A *branch* is a movable label on a line of commits, so work can go on there while the main
line, `main`, keeps working. To *push* is to copy commits to the shared repository on GitHub.
A *pull request* proposes merging a branch and shows the difference, or *diff*, line by line;
a *review* comments on it, approves it or asks for changes; *merging* adds its commits to
`main`.

Working alone, as in this book, you commit straight to `main` and push; in a team, every
change goes round the loop. Either way the assistant runs the Git commands and you approve
them. Ask it to "commit with a message that says why", and read its diffs before you approve:
a diff is the clearest check you have of what the assistant actually did.

## Where a site lives {#sec-hosting}

A rendered Quarto website is *static*: a folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and documents,
with no program running on a server. Any web server can serve it, so publishing means copying
that folder to a host. **GitHub Pages** is the host this book uses, because the repository is
already on GitHub and `quarto publish gh-pages` is built in (@fig-publish-flow).

![Publishing to GitHub Pages. The source goes to the `main` branch with Git; `quarto publish gh-pages` renders the site on your computer and pushes only the rendered HTML to a separate branch, which GitHub serves.](../media/diagrams/publish-flow){#fig-publish-flow .on-light fig-alt="Your project folder holds the source, which git pushes to the main branch of a GitHub repository. quarto publish gh-pages renders the site on your computer and pushes only the rendered HTML to a separate branch, gh-pages. GitHub Pages serves that branch at https://user.github.io/repo/. Anyone with the address can read the site."}

There are two ways to get a site onto a host. Either you render on your own computer and
upload the result, as `quarto publish` does for GitHub Pages and Netlify, or the host builds
the site from your repository on every push. The second works only if the build installs
Quarto, Python and every package the project needs, or if the rendered output is committed.
The London repository leaves its rendered `_site/` folder out, so a host that builds would
produce nothing until the build is set up.

::: practice
Free static hosts, checked on their official pages on 2026-11-07. Free plans change: read the
current limits before choosing.

| Host | How the site gets there | Note on the free plan |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub Pages | you upload: `quarto publish gh-pages` | the route in this book |
| Netlify | you upload: `quarto publish netlify` | 300 credits a month, 15 per production deploy; Quarto's Netlify build plugin runs no Python, so render locally |
| Cloudflare | you upload `_site/` with `wrangler deploy` | Pages allows 500 builds a month and 20,000 files |
| Vercel | the host builds from Git | Hobby plan: personal, non-commercial use only |
| GitLab Pages | the host builds, in a CI job | publishes a `public` folder: set `output-dir: public`, and install Quarto and Python in the job |
| Render | the host builds from Git | rebuilds on every push to the connected branch |

Quarto Pub, Quarto's own free host, is being replaced by Posit Connect Cloud.
:::

## One folder, one website {#sec-london-website}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Make this folder a Quarto website: _quarto.yml (render only the .qmd files; navbar: Guide, Dashboard, a Downloads menu for the docx, pdf, pptx, epub and london-slides.html files that exist), index.qmd, and a .gitignore for /_site/, /.quarto/, /.venv/ and *_files/. Render and check the links.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes 3 files · `uv run quarto render` → `_site/`
:::

::: {.you}
then, in the preview tab: Ctrl+C, and `uv run quarto preview`
:::

A `_quarto.yml` file at the top of the folder turns it into a *project*. `quarto render` with no
file name then builds every listed page into `_site/`, with shared navigation, and the dashboard
becomes one page of the site:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  render:                       # <1>
    - index.qmd
    - london.qmd
    - london-dashboard.qmd
website:
  title: "Visit London"
  navbar:
    left:
      - {text: Guide, href: london.qmd}
      - {text: Dashboard, href: london-dashboard.qmd}
      - {text: Downloads, menu: [...]}    # <2>
```
1. An explicit `render` list keeps the README, the data notes and the photo credits from
   becoming pages of the site.
2. The menu links the files the other formats wrote: the Word guide, the PDF, the flyer, and
   whichever optional files you made.

`.gitignore` lists what Git should not track: the rendered `_site/` (rebuilt from the source
and published separately), Quarto's working folder `.quarto/`, the environment `.venv/`
(rebuilt from `uv.lock`) and the `*_files/` folders of figures.

## Publish {#sec-london-publish}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Initialise a git repository here. Replace README.md in this folder with a short one linking to https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/ and listing the files in the site's Downloads menu. Commit everything except _site/, .quarto/, .venv/ and *_files/, then create a public GitHub repository named `london-guide` with gh and push to it. Set the repository's website to the same URL with `gh repo edit --homepage`. Show me the README and the website URL you set.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`git init` · `git add` · `git commit` · `gh repo create london-guide --public --source=. --push` · `gh repo edit --homepage …`
:::

::: {.you}
approve `gh` · in the second tab: `uv run quarto publish gh-pages`, then Enter at "Publish site … (Y/n)" · open the address on your phone · a 404? wait a minute and reload
:::

The assistant creates the repository on GitHub from your folder and pushes the commits, using
the sign-in from the setup check. Its README is the first thing visitors to the repository
see, and its link takes them on to the live site.

The first publish is yours, typed in the terminal. It asks one question, then renders the site,
creates the `gh-pages` branch, pushes the rendered site and opens it. Quarto's GitHub Pages guide
says to run `quarto publish gh-pages` locally, once, before setting up a GitHub Action to publish
(checked 2026-11-12). Make that first run interactive, too: in a dry run with Quarto 1.6.40,
`--no-prompt` stopped the first publish with "the remote origin does not have a branch named
gh-pages". That was observed with 1.6.40 and not re-tested with 1.10.20. Once the branch
exists, the assistant can update the site with `uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt`.

In that dry run, the first publish of each site took one and a half to two minutes, and GitHub
Pages then built it in 20 to 35 seconds, so a 404 page in the first minute usually means the
site is still being deployed.

::: pitfall
A push that fails with `HTTP 400` ("RPC failed", "the remote end hung up unexpectedly") was seen
with larger sites, such as dashboards with embedded maps. Raise Git's buffer for this repository
with `git config http.postBuffer 524288000`, and push again.
:::

::: practice
Publishing from your own computer is simple and keeps the build where your environment is. The
alternative, a GitHub Action that renders on every push (Quarto's
`quarto-dev/quarto-actions`), needs Python and the project's packages installed in the job,
or `freeze` set so that committed results are reused, and Quarto's guide still asks for one
local `quarto publish gh-pages` first.
:::

::: tryit
Publish the guide.

::: done
`https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/london-dashboard.html` opens on your
phone.
:::

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/README.md
```
:::
:::

## Change one input, explain the rebuild {#sec-london-change}

@sec-quarto began with a correction (@sec-drift): ALVA revises one figure, and in a
copy-and-paste workflow someone has to carry it by hand into every file that quotes it. Here
is that scenario for real, in a project where no visitor count was ever copied. No prompt is
supplied: write your own, or do it by hand.

::: tryit
1. **Predict.** Set the Tower of London's `visits_2025` in `data/attractions.csv` to `8000000`.
   Which outputs will change?
2. **Rebuild** the site.
3. **Explain** which outputs changed, which did not, and why.
4. **Undo**: `git restore data/attractions.csv`, then rebuild, so no trial number stays in your
   files.

Make the edit yourself (for example `nano data/attractions.csv`; Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X to save
and leave): the project's rules keep the assistant out of `data/`, which is the point of them.

::: done
you can name the outputs that changed, the ones that did not, and why.
:::
:::

The value is fictitious: chosen to change the top attraction, so that the effect is visible,
and reversible, because the publish step committed the real file.

To answer, you need to know which page reads which input. @tbl-london-deps is computed from the
finished project's sources: a page counts as reading a file only if its code loads it.

::: {#tbl-london-deps .cell tbl-cap='Which page of the finished London project (each a `.qmd` file) reads which file in `data/`, and the formats it writes. Computed from the sources: a mark means the page\'s code loads the file.' execution_count=2}
| Page | Writes | attrac­tions | visits | churches | sights |
|---|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| london | html, docx, pdf, pptx, epub, slides | ● |  |  |  |
| london-dashboard | html | ● | ● | ● |  |
| london-email | docx | ● |  |  |  |
| london-flyer | pdf |  |  |  |  |
| london-social | pdf | ● |  |  |  |
| london-whitepaper | pdf | ● | ● |  |  |
:::


In all, five pages load `attractions.csv`, and between them they write
ten files, so the change reaches all of them at the next render.
What it does there depends on each page's code. Of those pages, three
(the guide, the dashboard and the partner brief) find the top attraction with
`attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()` and the total with `.sum()`, so in each of them the Tower
of London becomes the most visited attraction and the total rises. The square advert uses only
the first call, so it names the Tower too. The white paper names no top attraction: its sums by
admission change, but its table keeps ALVA's `rank_uk` column from the file, which would still
rank the Tower ninth in the UK beside the most visits of the ten. A
copied column goes stale too. Still, that answers the question @sec-quarto began with: the
correction reaches ten files with one command, and nobody has to go
looking for them.

Copies deserve a second look. The flyer loads no data at all, and the sights tables in the
guide and the partner brief are typed, although the guide's credits name `sights.csv`: all
three *copy* their facts (price bands, nearest stations) from the cited file into the
Markdown. That was a reasonable choice, because those facts rarely change, but it means a
correction to `sights.csv` updates none of them. A cited copy is still a copy.

::: why
Why does every page recompute, even ones whose sources did not change? Because the project
renders with `freeze: false`: every render re-runs every page's code, which keeps this
exercise's answer simple. With caching turned on, a page whose own source did not change would
keep its old numbers, and the answer would depend on the cache; @sec-publish-many returns to
that trade-off.
:::

Two more things do not change: the live site, until you publish again
(`uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt`), and any output you did not rebuild. Model
answers, with the follow-up questions worth asking, are in @sec-checkpoints.

## A white paper (optional) {#sec-london-whitepaper}

The same data can also become an academic paper: an abstract, numbered sections, computed results
and a reference list, set in the typeface LaTeX documents use, without installing LaTeX.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create london-whitepaper.qmd, an A4 Typst white paper in "New Computer Modern": an abstract (no inline code), numbered Introduction, Methods, Results and Conclusions, then References via `#set bibliography(title: [References])` (references.bib from `url`). Analyse data/visits.csv vs 2019 and data/attractions.csv by `admission`. Add it to `render` and the "Downloads" menu; render; check citations. Figures must be vector: set `fig-format: svg` and check that the files in `figure-typst/` end in .svg.
```
:::

```yaml
bibliography: references.bib
format:
  typst:
    mainfont: "New Computer Modern"    # <1>
    section-numbering: "1.1"           # <2>
    bibliographystyle: ieee            # <3>
    fig-format: svg                    # <4>
```
1. Typst 0.15, bundled with Quarto 1.10.20, includes New Computer Modern, the OpenType version of
   LaTeX's Computer Modern, so the paper looks like a LaTeX article without a TeX installation.
2. Numbers the headings: 1, 1.1, 2.
3. Typst's numbered reference style; `[@key]` in the text cites an entry in `references.bib`.
4. Vector figures stay sharp at any zoom; the prompt's check makes sure they really are vectors.

![The first page of the finished London white paper: title, abstract, and numbered sections with citations. Rendered from `examples/london/london-whitepaper.qmd`.](../media/figures/london-whitepaper-p1.png){#fig-whitepaper width=75% .on-light fig-alt="The first page of an A4 paper set in a LaTeX-style typeface: the title Visits to London's leading ALVA member attractions, 2015 to 2025, the subtitle Pandemic loss and recovery: a descriptive analysis, the author London Tourism Office, an abstract, and sections 1, Introduction, and 2, Methods, with numbered citations in square brackets."}

::: pitfall
Three traps, all met while building the example. The paper's settings need Quarto 1.10 or newer:
Quarto 1.6.40's Typst rejects them with "unexpected argument: spacing". An inline expression in a
YAML `abstract` runs before the setup cell and fails, so the finished example writes its abstract
in the body, in a raw Typst block. And Typst prints its own heading above the reference list,
"Bibliography" by default, which the prompt changes with `#set bibliography(title: [References])`
so the paper needs no References heading of its own.
:::

A genuine LaTeX PDF is also available, as `format: pdf`, but it needs a TeX distribution, for
example `quarto install tinytex`. For most reports Typst is faster and simpler.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

Git keeps every version of the source as commits; teams move each change through branch, pull
request, review and merge. A rendered site is static files that any host can serve, and
`quarto publish gh-pages` fills GitHub Pages from your own computer, interactively the first
time. A `_quarto.yml` with an explicit render list makes a folder a website. When an input
changes, every page whose code loads it updates at the next render, in every format; copied
facts do not, and neither does the live site until you publish again.

That completes one guide for many audiences. In Part III the hard part is the analysis
itself: grouping Colombia's municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context.
That one analysis is then published as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all
reading the results of one script, and its rebuild test changes a setting of the analysis
instead of a number in a table.
